title: Now let me go in peace (Luke 2:21–35)
hook: Simeon holds the child and says he can die content; Mary is told a sword will pierce her soul

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherds heard the angel's evangelist-word on the night shift. Your line was great joy for all people. Who did you tell your good news to? Day five hundred ten.

Forty days after the birth, Joseph and Mary carry the baby up to the temple in Jerusalem, to do what the law of Moses asked of new parents. Luke tells us what they brought as an offering: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. That's a detail worth catching. The law allowed birds instead of a lamb for families who couldn't afford one. So this is a poor couple, in the crowded temple courts, with a newborn. Nobody is paying them any attention. Except one man. He's been waiting a long time for this exact moment, and he walks straight toward them.

His name is Simeon. In the King James Bible, he was "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him." It had been revealed to him that he would not die before he saw the Lord's Christ. So he takes the baby in his arms, and he sings. "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation." In Latin, it begins Nunc dimittis, now you dismiss, and that's its name. The Greek verb is the one used for releasing a servant from duty, or relieving a watchman at the end of his shift. Simeon has been standing watch his whole life. Now he's off duty. He can go home in peace. And he calls the child "A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." Both. For the nations and for his own people. A quick surprise here: Luke never says Simeon was old. We assume it because he's ready to die, and artists have always painted him with a white beard. The text just says he was waiting. Then he turns to Mary, and the song changes key. This child will cause the fall and rising of many, a sign that people will speak against, and then: "Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also." In the middle of the blessing, a warning. Christians have long heard in it the cross, and Mary standing near it. Catholic devotion remembers this as the first of Mary's sorrows. Joy and grief in one embrace, in a crowded temple, over a poor family's child.
screen: then, large: `NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end the day by saying Simeon's words. Right now, settle, and breathe, and look back over today. What did your eyes see that was good? A face, a kindness, a moment of light, even a small one. Name it. What are you still standing watch over, still carrying? Notice it, and imagine setting it down for the night, like a watchman going off duty. Tonight, before you sleep, if you pray, you can say Simeon's words: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word. If you don't, simply let the day be finished, and let yourself rest. The bell holds the time.
Nunc dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss: Simeon's song, holding the child, ready to go in peace because his eyes have seen.
Your line: depart in peace. Tonight, before sleep, name one good thing your eyes saw today, and then go off duty. Day five hundred ten.

howItsDone: Christians in many traditions say or sing the Nunc Dimittis at the end of the day, at Compline or Evensong, and many churches keep February 2 as the Presentation of the Lord, also called Candlemas.

original.note: Greek: you release, you dismiss. used for setting a servant free or relieving a watchman. in Latin, dimittis.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man saying he's ready to die.
what it means: a man who has stood watch his whole life holds the child and is released, in peace, and then warns Mary of a sword to come.
what a scholar hears: the verb for depart is the one for releasing a servant or relieving a watchman, and Luke never actually says Simeon was old.

notes: Forty days: the purification period after the birth of a son (Leviticus 12:2–4; Luke 2:22). Confirm.
The verb apolyō used for releasing a slave or dismissing a sentry: a common commentary observation. Confirm.
Simeon's age is not stated in Luke; tradition makes him old. Stated plainly.
Sorrows of Mary: Catholic devotion counts Simeon's prophecy as the first of the Seven Sorrows. Confirm.
Compline/Evensong use of the Nunc Dimittis and Candlemas on February 2. Confirm.
Practice invites saying a real text (Luke 2:29), offered as 'if you pray'.
